etymology: Formed within English by compounding green and horn, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence for the word in 1455. The OED lists uses in military contexts from the mid-1600s and for animals from the 1870s.
biblical_def: A greenhorn is a raw beginner: a man new to a trade, a place or a way of life, and easily taken in. The word is an old English compound of green, the colour of what is fresh and unripe, and horn. It is far older than the American frontier, where it became a stock word for the newcomer from the East. The Christian observation: Scripture has no contempt for the beginner, only for the beginner who will not learn. “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Pro 1:5), and “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9). But the green man is not to be put in charge too soon: an elder must be “Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6).
webster_summary: A raw, inexperienced newcomer, easily deceived; from green + horn (OED earliest 1455). Not a novice in office (1Ti 3:6).
webster_full: GREENHORN, n. (from 1455, OED) An inexperienced person; a newcomer unfamiliar with local ways and easily imposed upon. Compound of green + horn.
scriptures: Pro 1:5
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
corruption_summary: Every man starts green; the danger is the greenhorn who is given authority before he has learned, or who refuses to learn because he thinks he already knows.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul set a plain rule for the church: no novice in office (1Ti 3:6). The reason is not that beginners are worthless but that early promotion feeds pride. A congregation that hands its pulpit or its board to the newest enthusiast has forgotten the rule.

The beginner has his own temptation, which is to believe whatever he is told: “The simple believeth every word” (Pro 14:15). The cure for being green is the word of God, which “giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).
roots_lines: 1455: OED’s earliest evidence for the word
usage: “Every hand on the ranch had been a greenhorn once.”
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning. (Pro 1:5).

etymology: Formed within English by compounding tender and foot, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1881, in the writing of Linus Brockett. The OED lists uses in education from the 1880s and in scouting from the 1900s.
biblical_def: A tenderfoot is a newcomer not yet hardened to rough living: in the American West, the new arrival not yet used to the country, and later the first rank of a Boy Scout. The compound is plain: a man whose feet are still tender, not yet toughened by the trail. The Christian observation: Scripture expects the believer to be hardened by use, not to stay tender-footed. “But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil” (Heb 5:14). Hardening comes by walking, and the walking is learned under instruction: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9).
webster_summary: A newcomer not yet hardened to rough life; later the first Scout rank; from tender + foot (OED earliest 1881). Senses exercised by use (Heb 5:14).
webster_full: TENDERFOOT, n. (from 1881, OED) A newcomer unaccustomed to hardship or to the ways of a place; in scouting, a beginner’s rank. Compound of tender + foot.
scriptures: Heb 5:14
But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: The tenderfoot was expected to toughen on the trail; the error of a soft age is to shield the young from the walking that would harden them.
corruption_paragraphs: The word assumed a change: tender feet become hard by use. A culture that removes every hardship from the young keeps them tender-footed into manhood, and then wonders why they cannot walk far.
Hebrews says maturity comes “by reason of use” (Heb 5:14). Fathers and churches harden their young by giving them real work and real instruction, not by sparing them the trail.
roots_summary: tender + foot → tenderfoot (OED earliest 1881) → Western newcomer → first Scout rank (OED: scouting, 1900s).
usage: “He was a tenderfoot his first winter and a hand by spring.”
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser. (Pro 9:9).

etymology: A borrowing from Spanish estampida, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1828. The OED lists uses in agriculture and of animals from the 1820s, in mining and United States politics from the 1840s.
biblical_def: A stampede is the sudden, panicked rush of a herd, cattle or horses, all running at once; by extension, any headlong rush of a crowd. The word came into English from Spanish estampida. The OED records it in American politics from the 1840s, for a sudden rush of voters or delegates. The Christian observation: a herd stampedes because each animal runs because the others run. Scripture describes the panic of the guilty: “The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion” (Pro 28:1). And it names the cure: “In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength” (Isa 30:15). “The fear of man bringeth a snare” (Pro 29:25).
webster_summary: A sudden panicked rush of a herd; any headlong rush of a crowd; from Spanish estampida (OED earliest 1828). In quietness and confidence shall be your strength (Isa 30:15).
webster_full: STAMPEDE, n. (from 1828, OED) A sudden rush of frightened animals; any sudden mass movement of people. v. To rush in panic, or to cause to. From Spanish estampida.
scriptures: Pro 28:1
The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
corruption_summary: A herd stampedes on fear, not on reasons; the political and social stampede does the same, and the man who runs because everyone runs has handed his judgment to the herd.
corruption_paragraphs: The OED records stampede in American politics by the 1840s, and every generation since has seen its rushes: panics, manias, moral fads. Each animal in a stampede is reacting to the others, not to the danger. A crowd can run a long way on nothing but its own noise.

Scripture asks the believer to stand still when the herd runs. Quietness and confidence are his strength (Isa 30:15), and the fear of man is a snare (Pro 29:25). The righteous are bold as a lion because they answer to God, not to the crowd (Pro 28:1).
roots_summary: Spanish estampida → stampede (OED earliest 1828) → panicked herd → mining rushes and political rushes (OED, 1840s).
roots_lines: 1820s: OED subjects agriculture and animals; 1840s: mining, United States politics
usage: “The thunder set off a stampede, and they lost forty head.”
The fear of man bringeth a snare. (Pro 29:25).

etymology: A borrowing from Spanish lazo, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1808, in the Narrative of the Expedition under General Craufurd. The OED lists uses in agriculture from the 1800s.
biblical_def: A lasso is a long rope with a running noose at one end, thrown to catch cattle or horses; to lasso is to catch an animal with one. The word came into English from Spanish lazo, a noose or snare. The Christian observation: a rope can drag or it can draw. Scripture uses the cord both ways. God says of Israel, “I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love” (Hos 11:4). The rope that catches a straying animal is a picture of the Shepherd who goes after the lost and brings it home: “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring” (Joh 10:16).
webster_summary: A rope with a running noose for catching cattle or horses; from Spanish lazo (OED earliest 1808). Drawn with cords of a man, with bands of love (Hos 11:4).
webster_full: LASSO, n. (from 1808, OED) A long rope with a running noose, used to catch animals. v. To catch with a lasso. From Spanish lazo.
scriptures: Hos 11:4
I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
corruption_summary: A lasso brings the stray home by force; God’s cords are “bands of love”, and the error is to think He only ropes and drags.
corruption_paragraphs: Some imagine God’s sovereignty as a rope thrown over an unwilling animal. Hosea describes it differently: cords of a man, bands of love (Hos 11:4). God’s drawing is effectual, but it works through love, not mere force.
The Shepherd does go after His sheep and bring them in (Joh 10:16). The church is not to be passive about the strays; it goes out after them with the same bands of love.
roots_summary: Spanish lazo, noose → lasso (OED earliest 1808) → cattleman’s rope → verb, to rope an animal.
roots_lines: 1808: OED’s earliest evidence, Narrative of the Expedition under General Craufurd
usage: “He could lasso a calf at a dead run.”
I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love. (Hos 11:4).

etymology: A borrowing from Spanish corral, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence for the word in 1582, in a translation by Nicholas Lichefield. The OED lists uses in agriculture from the late 1500s, hunting from the late 1700s, and fortification from the 1840s.
biblical_def: A corral is a pen or enclosure for horses or cattle; to corral is to drive animals into one, and by extension to gather and confine people or things. The word came into English from Spanish corral. The OED records a fortification sense from the 1840s as well. The Christian observation: Scripture’s enclosure is the sheepfold, and it has one door. “He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber” (Joh 10:1). God promises to gather His people “as the flock in the midst of their fold” (Mic 2:12), and Christ promises “one fold, and one shepherd” (Joh 10:16).
webster_summary: A pen for horses or cattle; to drive into one, or to round up; from Spanish corral (OED earliest 1582). One fold, and one shepherd (Joh 10:16).
webster_full: CORRAL, n. (from 1582, OED) An enclosure for livestock. v. To drive into a corral; to gather and confine. From Spanish corral.
scriptures: Joh 10:1
Verily, verily, I say unto you, He that entereth not by the door into the sheepfold, but climbeth up some other way, the same is a thief and a robber.
Mic 2:12

I will surely assemble, O Jacob, all of thee; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as the flock in the midst of their fold: they shall make great noise by reason of the multitude of men.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
corruption_summary: A corral holds animals for the owner’s use; Christ’s fold holds His sheep for their safety, and men who corral consciences for their own ends are climbing in some other way.
corruption_paragraphs: Men are good at corralling one another: into parties, movements and causes that use them. Christ warns against the one who enters the fold “some other way” (Joh 10:1); he wants the sheep, but not for their good.
The true fold has one door and one Shepherd (Joh 10:16), and He gathers the flock to keep it, not to spend it (Mic 2:12).
roots_summary: Spanish corral → corral (OED earliest 1582) → livestock pen → verb, to round up.
roots_lines: 1582: OED’s earliest evidence, translation by Nicholas Lichefield
usage: “Corral the horses before the storm hits.”
And there shall be one fold, and one shepherd. (Joh 10:16).

etymology: Probably a borrowing from Spanish mestengo or mostrenco, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1808, in the writing of Zebulon Pike, soldier and explorer. The OED’s “probably” marks the source as not certain.
biblical_def: A mustang is a small, hardy, half-wild horse of the American plains. The OED derives the word, probably, from Spanish mestengo or mostrenco, and first records it in the writing of the explorer Zebulon Pike in 1808. It lists uses for horses from the 1800s and in military contexts from the 1840s. The Christian observation: a wild horse is strong and beautiful, and useless to a rider until it is broken. Scripture uses the untamed horse as a warning: “Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle” (Psa 32:9). Israel’s sin is pictured the same way: “every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle” (Jer 8:6).
webster_summary: A small, hardy, half-wild horse of the plains; probably from Spanish mestengo (OED earliest 1808, Zebulon Pike). Be ye not as the horse which has no understanding (Psa 32:9).
webster_full: MUSTANG, n. (from 1808, OED) A small, hardy, half-wild horse of the American plains. Probably from Spanish mestengo or mostrenco (OED).
scriptures: Psa 32:9
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
Jer 8:6
I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength.
corruption_summary: The mustang is admired for being unbroken; the culture admires the same in men, but Scripture says the man who must be held in with bit and bridle has no understanding.
corruption_paragraphs: Wildness is romantic in a horse and in a slogan. The free, unbroken spirit is held up as the ideal, and restraint is treated as loss. Scripture sees an unbroken will as folly, not freedom (Psa 32:9).
Strength is not safety either: “An horse is a vain thing for safety” (Psa 33:17). The believer’s strength is a will brought under God, which goes where it is told without needing the bridle.
roots_summary: Probably Spanish mestengo / mostrenco → mustang (OED earliest 1808, Zebulon Pike) → wild plains horse.
roots_lines: 1800s: OED subject horses and riding; 1840s: military
usage: “They ran a band of mustangs into the canyon.”
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding. (Psa 32:9).

etymology: A borrowing from Spanish bronco, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1861, in the writing of J. R. Browne.
biblical_def: A bronco is an untamed or half-tamed horse of the American West, one that bucks and fights the rider. The word came into English from Spanish bronco, and the OED first records it in 1861. Breaking a bronco is a test of patience and nerve, and the rider who does it controls the whole animal through a small piece of iron. The Christian observation: James uses exactly that picture for the tongue. “Behold, we put bits in the horses’ mouths, that they may obey us; and we turn about their whole body” (Jas 3:3). The Psalmist warns against being like the horse that must be held in with bit and bridle (Psa 32:9).
webster_summary: An untamed or half-tamed horse of the West; from Spanish bronco (OED earliest 1861). We put bits in the horses’ mouths (Jas 3:3).
webster_full: BRONCO, n. (from 1861, OED) An untamed or imperfectly broken horse of the western United States. From Spanish bronco.
scriptures: Jas 3:3
Behold, we put bits in the horses' mouths, that they may obey us; and we turn about their whole body.
Psa 32:9
Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee.
corruption_summary: A bronco is turned by a small bit; James says the tongue is the same, and the man who will not bridle it has an unbroken life.
corruption_paragraphs: The bronco buster knows that the whole horse follows the mouth. James applies it to men: a small member steers the whole body (Jas 3:3). Our age has made unbridled speech a virtue, as if the bucking were the point.
The Christian is to be broken to God’s word so that he does not need the bit and bridle of outward force (Psa 32:9).
roots_summary: Spanish bronco → bronco (OED earliest 1861, J. R. Browne) → untamed Western horse.
roots_lines: 1861: OED’s earliest evidence, J. R. Browne
usage: “He stayed on the bronco for the full eight seconds.”
Behold, we put bits in the horses' mouths, that they may obey us. (Jas 3:3).

etymology: Probably an arbitrary formation, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which records its earliest evidence in 1829, in the Virginia Literary Museum. In other words, it is a made-up word with no traceable parts.
biblical_def: To hornswoggle is to cheat, hoax or swindle someone. The OED treats it as probably an arbitrary formation, a coined word with no known parts, and first records it in 1829 in a Virginia magazine. It belongs to the family of comic American coinages of that era. The comedy of the word does not soften the thing it names. The Christian observation: Scripture calls the swindle what it is. “That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such” (1Th 4:6). “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel” (Pro 20:17). “A false balance is abomination to the LORD” (Pro 11:1).
webster_summary: To cheat or swindle; probably an arbitrary coinage (OED earliest 1829, Virginia Literary Museum). The Lord is the avenger of all such (1Th 4:6).
webster_full: HORNSWOGGLE, v.t. (from 1829, OED) To cheat, hoax or swindle. Probably an arbitrary formation (OED).
scriptures: That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.
Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: A funny word for fraud makes the fraud sound like a game; Scripture says the Lord avenges the man defrauded.
corruption_paragraphs: Comic words for cheating, such as hornswoggle, bamboozle and con, let us laugh at a swindle as if the victim were only a fool. But the victim is a brother, and the Lord is his avenger (1Th 4:6).
The sweetness of deceit is short. Solomon says the bread turns to gravel (Pro 20:17).
roots_summary: Probably arbitrary coinage → hornswoggle (OED earliest 1829, Virginia Literary Museum) → to cheat or hoax.
usage: “Don’t let that salesman hornswoggle you on the trade-in.”
Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel. (Pro 20:17).
